stem: Series A has mean 50 and CV 20%. Series B has mean 80 and CV 15%. Which series is more consistent?

options.text: Series A, because its CV is higher
Series B, because its CV is lower
Series A, because its mean is lower
Series B, because its standard deviation is lower

per_option_rationale.rationale: Confuses the direction: higher CV means MORE variability, hence LESS consistency, not more.
Lower CV indicates less relative variability. Series B (CV = 15%) is more consistent than Series A (CV = 20%).
Uses the mean instead of CV to judge consistency; the mean indicates the level, not the spread relative to the mean.

SD of B = 0.15 x 80 = 12; SD of A = 0.20 x 50 = 10. Series A actually has a lower absolute SD, so this claim is factually wrong and uses an inappropriate measure for comparing series with different means.

explanation: Consistency is measured by the coefficient of variation (CV). A lower CV means smaller relative spread. Series B has CV = 15% versus Series A at CV = 20%, so Series B is more consistent. Comparing absolute SDs is incorrect when means differ.

explanation_sections.punchline: Lower CV means more consistency - CV, not SD, is the correct comparator when means differ.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the measure for comparing consistency across series with different means: use CV. Compare directly: CV_A = 20%, CV_B = 15%. Lower CV wins for consistency, so Series B.
explanation_sections.lesson: For comparing variability across groups with different means or units, always use CV, not absolute SD.
explanation_sections.timing: About 30 seconds. Recall the rule: lower CV = more consistent. The trap is option 4 which computes actual SDs (A=10, B=12) and picks A - but absolute SD comparison is wrong here.
